title: Chapter 5: He Came Back Married
content: Ruthie sets the cup down and pours before Wren has taken her coat off, and says, "You look like a woman who has been sitting in a plastic chair for two days."
"Three," Wren says.
"Three." Ruthie puts the pot back on the burner. "Then you need eggs."

The Bend Diner at noon is nine stools and four booths and a pie case with a cracked corner that Ruthie has never replaced because the crack is on the side nobody looks at. The windows are fogged at the bottom. It smells like bacon and burnt coffee and the wet wool of everybody's coats drying on the backs of the chairs.

The ferry is tied up at the landing with the cable slack in the water. There is nothing to run. The Authority has the landing marked with a sawhorse and a paper sign in a plastic sleeve, and the paper sign has been rained on twice and the ink has run so that the word NOTICE looks like NOTHING.

Wren has been at the Annex since Monday. She has been in the diner every day since Sunday because the house at 9 Ferry Lane is too quiet to sit in, and Ruthie does not ask her questions, which is a form of kindness that Wren can accept.

Two men at the end of the counter are talking about the high school football team. A booth of line workers is talking about the gate. Neither conversation touches hers, and she sits in the middle of both.
Ruthie takes the pencil off the string and opens the composition book under the register.
"You writing me down," Wren says.
"I write down what I hear," Ruthie says. "It saves arguing later."
The door opens and the bell over it goes off, and Wren looks up because everybody looks up, and Theo Marsh is standing in the doorway with the light behind him and a woman on his arm.

He is wearing a jacket she has seen before, a canvas jacket with a torn pocket. He is wearing it over a shirt with a collar, and clipped to the pocket is a badge on a blue lanyard, and the badge says T. MARSH, FIELD ENGINEER, DISTRICT 4, and there is a photograph on it of a man who looks younger than the man in the doorway.

The woman is tall and has her hair pulled back and a cardigan over her shoulders like a coat left on the back of a chair. She is looking around the diner the way people look around a room they have been told about.

That was two summers ago, and it was not a romance anybody in this town would have recognized. He came in June to survey the east landing and stayed until the light went. He left a jacket on the hook by her door and took it back in October without a word. She learned the shape of his handwriting from a grocery list he wrote on the back of a survey sheet, and she could still draw it from memory if anybody asked, which nobody has.
Ruthie looks at the door, then at Wren, then at the door.
"Table four's clean," Ruthie says, loud enough for the room.
Theo does not move to table four. He stands in the doorway with his hand still on the door and says, "Wren."
She has her cup in both hands. She does not put it down.

He crosses the floor. The woman comes with him, half a step behind, and when he stops at the counter she stops beside him and puts her hand out, and Wren sees the ring before she sees the hand, because the ring catches the light from the window.
"You're Wren," the woman says. "I'm Celia. Celia Reeve."
Wren takes the hand. It is a good handshake, dry and quick, and it is not a performance.
"I'm so sorry about your grandfather," Celia says. "Theo told me. I've been thinking about you all week."
"Thank you," Wren says.
"He was in the water," Celia says. "That's what I heard. That he was in the water when it came up."
"He drowned," Wren says.
Celia's hand stops halfway back to her cardigan.
"There's a difference in this town," Wren says. "In the water is weather. Drowned is a cause. I need the second one."
The diner has gone quiet in the way a diner goes quiet, which is not silent, because the fryer is still going and somebody at the end of the counter is still chewing.

The oldest man in the room puts his cup down in the saucer. He has been coming here since the diner had a different name and a different owner and a counter with a brass rail on it, and he has not said a word all morning.
"He drowned," the old man says. "I was at the landing. I saw the boat come in sideways."
Nobody argues with him. The line worker in the booth looks at his plate.
Ruthie leans on the counter with the pencil in her fist. "Say the rest of it," she says.
"There isn't any rest of it," the old man says. "That's the whole of it. He drowned and nobody will write it down."

Ruthie writes it down. She writes slowly, with her tongue between her teeth, and when she is done she turns the book around so the old man can see it, and he reads it and nods, once, and goes back to his cup.
Theo says, "Celia."
"I'm all right," Celia says. She says it to him, not to Wren, and then she says to Wren, "That's fair."
Ruthie turns to a clean page. She licks the lead, which she does not need to do, and says, "Spell it for me."
"Spell what," Celia says.
"Reeve," Ruthie says. "Two e's at the end, or one?"
"Two."
"Same as the director," Ruthie says, and writes it.
Celia's face does something small and quick and then is smooth again. "She's my mother."
"I know she is," Ruthie says, and writes that down too, and underlines it, and closes the book.
"Can I ask you something," Celia says. "Not about any of this. About the boat."
Wren looks at her.
"How does it work," Celia says. "The cable. I've seen it from the bluff but I've never understood what holds it up."

"Nothing holds it up," Wren says. "It lies on the bottom between the towers. The drum takes it in and the boat walks itself along it. The cable's job is to keep you from going downstream. It's not a rail. It's a leash."
"And the nine?"

"Nine passengers, rated. Not because nine is safe. Because nine is what the hull was built for in 1908 and nobody has ever re-rated it, and if you put fourteen on it in a following wind you can bury the bow to the gunwale."
Celia thinks about that. "Who decides it's nine?"
"Nobody decides it," Wren says. "It's painted on the hull. Somebody painted it in 1908 and everybody since has agreed."
Celia looks at her coffee. "That's the whole system?"
"That's the whole system," Wren says. "It works because everyone agrees. That's true of most things here."
Ruthie makes a sound that could be a laugh if it were friendlier.

Theo has not sat down. He is standing with one hand on the back of the stool beside Wren, the third stool, the one her grandfather took every morning for fifty-one years, and he does not know that, and she is not going to tell him.
"How long are you in town," Wren says.
"Through the weekend." He says it to the counter. "There's a gate inspection. Structural, plus the actuators. It's on the calendar from last spring."
"Last spring," she says.
"March."
"And nobody moved it."
"Nobody moved it," he says.
Ruthie puts a cup in front of him without being asked and he wraps both hands around it, and Wren watches him do it and remembers the hands. The nail on the left thumb is still short. He bites it.
Celia has taken the stool on the other side of him and is looking at the menu, which she does not need, because the menu is one page and laminated and says what it has said since 1994.
"Your file came across my desk Monday," Theo says.
Wren waits.
"Incident at Mile 9. One fatality. Cause pending."
"Pending is a word I know," she says.
"It's not a word I put there."
"Somebody did."
He turns the cup a quarter turn on the counter. "It's a routing field. It defaults."
"Then somebody didn't change it."
Celia has put the menu down. She is looking at Wren now with an expression Wren cannot file, and it is not pity, and it is not amusement, and it is close to attention.
"Theo," Celia says. "Tell her the other thing."

Theo takes a breath and lets it out. "I pulled the file. I can't stamp it. I'm not a certifying officer, I'm an engineer, and certifying officers are in Columbus and there are four of them and they have a backlog going back to the flood."
"Then what can you do," Wren says.
"I can read it myself," he says.
Ruthie snorts, from the far end, where she is wiping a cup she has already wiped.
"The inspection," Wren says. "Is that why they ran the gate on the twelfth. To move the silt ahead of it."
"That's not how it works," Theo says.
"Then how does it work."
"The gate pulses when the sediment load crosses a threshold. It's scheduled at the start of the release season, out of Columbus. The district doesn't set the date."
"Somebody sets the date."
"Somebody does," he says, and looks at his cup.
Wren puts her cup down.
"I'll look at your file personally," Theo says. "Monday. Before I fly back. That's not nothing. A field engineer's note on a file moves it up the stack. It's not a stamp, but it's a note."
"Whose stack."
"Ottoline's, eventually."
"Eventually," Wren says.
He does not answer that.
Celia says, quietly, "He's trying."
"I know he is," Wren says. "That's what I'm afraid of."

She takes the last of her coffee and puts two dollars on the counter, and Ruthie pushes it back with one finger and says, "Your money's no good here this week," and Wren does not argue, because arguing costs more than two dollars.
She stands and puts her coat on and buttons it and takes her folder off the counter, and she does it slowly, so that they have to stand there and watch her do it.
At the counter the old man lifts his cup an inch off the saucer, which is what passes here for a salute. Wren lifts her folder an inch. Neither of them says anything.
At the door she turns around.
"Monday," she says. "In the morning. Not the afternoon."
"In the morning," Theo says.
"It's in Columbus," she says. "The file."
"I know," he says. "I put it in my bag."
highlight: Theo Marsh walks into the diner with Celia Reeve and a district badge and says the file is in Columbus.
